overview.title: What TensorBoard does and how to launch it from fit()
overview.section: 7.3 Using built-in training and evaluation loops
overview.main_topic: TensorBoard's capabilities, the keras.callbacks.TensorBoard callback, and starting a local TensorBoard server
overview.central_idea: TensorBoard is a locally run, browser-based app for monitoring training. With Keras you enable it by adding keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir=...) to fit()'s callbacks; the callback writes logs to that directory, and running `tensorboard --logdir <dir>` serves the interface at a URL.
overview.importance: It turns the abstract 'results -> idea' arc of figure 7.6 (p.236) into a concrete two-step recipe you will use for every non-trivial training run.
learning_objectives: List the four TensorBoard capabilities named on the page
Explain why monitoring more than the final loss speeds progress
Add a TensorBoard callback to fit() with a log directory
Launch the TensorBoard server from the command line and know how to install it if missing
prerequisites: get_mnist_model() and the MNIST split from section 7.3

summary:
TensorBoard is described as "a browser-based application that you can run locally" and "the best way to monitor everything that goes on inside your model during training". With it you can:

- visually monitor metrics during training,
- visualize your model architecture,
- visualize histograms of activations and gradients,
- explore embeddings in 3D.

The authors argue that monitoring more than the model's final loss gives a clearer picture of what the model does and doesn't do, and lets you make progress more quickly.

The easiest integration with `fit()` is the **`keras.callbacks.TensorBoard`** callback: in the simplest case you only specify where logs should be written. The code builds and compiles the MNIST model (Adam, sparse categorical crossentropy, accuracy), creates `tensorboard = keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir="/full_path_to_your_log_dir")`, and calls `fit()` for 10 epochs with validation data and `callbacks=[tensorboard]`.

Once training starts, logs are written to the target location. On a local machine you launch the server with `tensorboard --logdir /full_path_to_your_log_dir`; the `tensorboard` executable should already be present if TensorFlow was installed via `pip`, otherwise install it with `pip install tensorboard`. Then open the URL the command prints. For Colab, an embedded TensorBoard can run inside the notebook - the commands for that are on p.238.

paragraphs.excerpt: TensorBoard is a browser-based application that you can run locally. It’s the best
paragraphs.what_it_says: TensorBoard runs locally and is viewed in a browser; the authors call it the best way to monitor everything inside a model during training. Four capabilities are listed: visually monitoring metrics during training, visualizing model architecture, visualizing histograms of activations and gradients, and exploring embeddings in 3D.
paragraphs.what_it_means: TensorBoard reads event files written during training and renders dashboards: scalar curves (loss/metrics per epoch), a graph view of the model, distributions of tensor values over time, and a projector for embedding vectors (e.g. via PCA or t-SNE).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Each capability answers a different debugging question: Is it learning/overfitting? Is the architecture what I think? Are activations saturating or gradients vanishing? What structure has the model learned?
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: histograms and embeddings must be explicitly enabled in the Keras callback (e.g. histogram_freq=1); the default configuration logs scalars (and the graph where the backend supports it).

terminology.meaning: Distribution of the values of a layer's outputs or gradients, plotted per epoch to show how it evolves.
TensorBoard view that projects high-dimensional vectors to 3D for interactive exploration.

concepts.name: TensorBoard
concepts.definition: A browser-based application, run locally, for monitoring training: metrics, model architecture, activation/gradient histograms, 3D embeddings.
concepts.intuition: An instrument panel for your training run.
concepts.technical: A server process reads event files from --logdir and renders dashboards.
concepts.significance: Speeds up the results -> idea arc of the loop of progress.
concepts.misconception: It is not tied to training in TensorFlow; Keras writes the logs regardless of backend.

concepts.name: keras.callbacks.TensorBoard
concepts.definition: Built-in callback that writes training logs for TensorBoard to log_dir.
concepts.technical: At epoch end (and optionally batches) it writes the metric values from logs to event files; options enable histograms, graph, profiling.
concepts.significance: The easiest way to use TensorBoard with fit().
concepts.misconception: Creating the callback does not launch the viewer; you still start the tensorboard server.

concepts.name: Keras callback
concepts.definition: Object passed to fit() and called at training events.
concepts.significance: TensorBoard integration is implemented as one.

code.title: Training with the TensorBoard callback
code.original_code:
model = get_mnist_model()
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)

tensorboard = keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(
    log_dir="/full_path_to_your_log_dir",
)
model.fit(
    train_images,
    train_labels,
    epochs=10,
    validation_data=(val_images, val_labels),
    callbacks=[tensorboard],
)
code.what_it_does: Trains the MNIST model for 10 epochs while writing TensorBoard logs (train and validation metrics) to the given directory.

line_explanations.explanation: Build and compile the model, same configuration as earlier in section 7.3.

parameters.name: log_dir
parameters.role: Where event files are written; the same path is given to --logdir.

pitfalls: Replace the placeholder path with a real directory.
Reusing one log_dir for several runs mixes their curves; use subfolders per run.
Without validation_data, no validation curves appear.

# AI-written variant (not in the book): one subfolder per run, with histograms
import datetime
run_dir = "logs/" + datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
tensorboard = keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir=run_dir, histogram_freq=1)

code.what_it_does: Starts the TensorBoard web server reading the log directory and prints a URL to open in a browser.

line_explanations.explanation: Shell command (not Python); --logdir must point to the callback's log_dir.

deeper.title: What each TensorBoard view helps diagnose
deeper.body:
| View (from the bullet list) | Typical question it answers |
|---|---|
| Metrics during training | Is the model learning? When does validation loss start rising (overfitting)? |
| Model architecture | Are layers connected as intended? Are shapes right? |
| Histograms of activations and gradients | Are ReLUs dying, activations saturating, gradients vanishing/exploding? |
| Embeddings in 3D | Do similar inputs cluster together in the learned representation? |

(Interpretation added beyond the book.)

deeper.title: Two processes, one directory
deeper.body:
1. Your training script runs `fit()`; the TensorBoard callback appends events to `log_dir`.
2. In a separate terminal you run `tensorboard --logdir <same dir>`.
3. The server watches the directory; your browser polls the server; curves update while training continues.

Because the only link is the directory, you can also copy logs from a remote machine and view them locally.

misconceptions.claim: Adding keras.callbacks.TensorBoard to fit() opens the TensorBoard interface.
misconceptions.correction: The callback only writes logs; you must launch the server (tensorboard --logdir ...) or the Colab magic (p.238) and open its URL.
The book says it is a browser-based application you run locally.

misconceptions.claim: You need TensorFlow as the Keras backend to use TensorBoard.
misconceptions.correction: The callback writes log files regardless of backend; the tensorboard package only needs to be installed (pip install tensorboard).

takeaways: TensorBoard is a locally run, browser-based monitoring app.
It shows training metrics, model architecture, activation/gradient histograms and 3D embeddings.
Use keras.callbacks.TensorBoard(log_dir=...) in fit(callbacks=[...]) to write logs.
View them with `tensorboard --logdir <dir>` (install with pip install tensorboard if needed) and open the printed URL.
Monitoring more than the final loss helps you understand the model and iterate faster.

options: TensorBoard refuses to run without it

questions.answer: So that validation metrics are computed and logged alongside training metrics
questions.explanation: Validation metrics only exist when validation data is provided; the callback then logs them as a separate run. The callback itself works without it, and log_dir/histograms are callback options.
